This repository already contains `bookmarks`, a command-line bookmark manager that stores bookmarks in SQLite. Read the existing code and any documentation in the repository before changing it. Add the two features below; every existing command must keep working exactly as it does now. 1. **Import.** `python -m bookmarks [--db PATH] import FILE --format csv|json` reads bookmarks from FILE in the same formats that `export` writes: CSV with the header row `id,url,title,tags`, or a JSON array of objects with the keys `url`, `title` and `tags` (a list of strings). Each bookmark in the file is added exactly as the `add` command would add it, with the same rules for URLs, titles and tags. The `id` in the file is ignored, and new ids are assigned as usual. When it finishes it prints `imported N` to standard output, where N is the number of bookmarks added. If FILE cannot be read, or is not valid CSV or JSON of that shape, it prints an error message to standard error, imports nothing, and exits with status 2. 2. **HTML export.** `export --format html` prints all bookmarks, ordered by id, as an HTML page in this form: ``` Bookmarks
  • TITLE TAGS
``` with one `
  • ` line per bookmark, where TAGS are the bookmark's tags joined with commas in alphabetical order. Examples, with a file `in.json` containing `[{"url": "https://docs.python.org", "title": "Python docs", "tags": ["python", "docs"]}, {"url": "https://example.com", "title": "Example", "tags": []}]` and an empty database (`` stands for a tab character): ``` $ python -m bookmarks --db b.db import in.json --format json imported 2 $ python -m bookmarks --db b.db list 1https://docs.python.orgPython docsdocs,python 2https://example.comExample $ python -m bookmarks --db b.db export --format html (an HTML page that contains Python docs) ```

Done. Both features are in, with all 32 pre-existing tests still passing (61 total now).

## What I added

**`src/bookmarks/cli.py`**
- `import FILE --format csv|json` (`cmd_import` + `read_import_file`/`read_csv`/`read_json`). The whole file is parsed and validated *before* anything is stored, so a bad file imports nothing; on success it prints `imported N`.
- CSV requires the exact `id,url,title,tags` header and 4-field rows; the `id` column is ignored and the tags cell goes through the same `parse_tags` the `add` command uses. JSON requires a top-level array of objects with a `url`; `title`/`tags` default to `""`/`[]` as in `add`, and tags are stripped, de-duplicated and sorted.
- `export --format html` (`write_html`) emits exactly the page from the spec, with `html.escape` on the URL (quoted, for the attribute) and on the title and tag text.

**`src/bookmarks/storage.py`** — `Store.add_many()`, which inserts a batch in one transaction so the all-or-nothing guarantee also survives a database error mid-import.

**`tests/test_bookmarks.py`** — 29 new tests: the spec's worked example, export↔import round trips for both formats (including embedded quotes/commas and unicode), id assignment after import, HTML ordering/escaping/empty-page, and 15 rejection cases each asserting exit 2, empty stdout, non-empty stderr and an unchanged database.

## One judgment call worth flagging

The spec says each bookmark is added "with the same rules for URLs" but only describes exit 2 for files that are unreadable or malformed. I read a non-`http(s)` URL inside the file as making the file unusable: it prints an error to stderr, imports **nothing** (not even the valid entries before it), and exits 2 — the same status `add` uses for a bad URL. The alternative would be to skip bad rows and count the rest, which would conflict with "imports nothing" on error; tell me if you want that behaviour instead.

Existing commands are untouched apart from `export` gaining `html` in its `--format` choices. I haven't committed anything.
